name: Gwaii Haanas National Park Reserve, National Marine Conservation Area Reserve, and Haida Heritage Site
blurb: Salmon, bears and seabirds linking Haida rainforest to the sea.

tip.title: Remove the salmon
tip.text: Salmon feed bears, eagles, sea lions and orcas, and their carcasses feed ravens and the forest. Set Pacific salmon to -100% and watch the predators on land and at sea.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Gwaii Haanas National Park Reserve and Haida Heritage Site

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Light drives the growth of rainforest trees on land and of kelp and plankton in the sea.

nodes.name: Heavy Pacific rain
nodes.desc: Wet maritime weather feeds the temperate rainforest and the many streams and lakes that run to the sea.

nodes.name: Cool nutrient-rich ocean water
nodes.desc: Cool, nutrient-bearing water from the open Pacific supports plankton, kelp and the animals that feed on them.

nodes.name: Fungi and bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down fallen trees, salmon carcasses and dead marine life, returning nutrients to soil and water.

nodes.name: Sitka spruce
nodes.desc: A large conifer of the coastal rainforest. Bald eagles nest in big coastal trees like it.

nodes.name: Western red cedar
nodes.desc: Dominant rainforest conifer in Gwaii Haanas. Browsed by introduced deer, which can limit young cedars.

nodes.name: Salal
nodes.desc: Evergreen shrub of the forest understory with berries; understory plants like it are browsed by deer.

nodes.name: Bull kelp
nodes.desc: Canopy kelp that forms forests in cool coastal water. Parks Canada and Haida partners work on kelp restoration here.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Drifting microscopic algae that feed zooplankton and krill. General ecological knowledge.

nodes.name: Sitka black-tailed deer
nodes.desc: Introduced to Haida Gwaii, now abundant, and browses native plants heavily. With no wolves on the islands, bears and hunters are the main predators.

nodes.name: Red sea urchin
nodes.desc: Grazes kelp. Without sea otters, which were hunted out in the fur trade, urchins can multiply and threaten kelp forests.

nodes.name: Krill and zooplankton
nodes.desc: Small drifting crustaceans that eat phytoplankton and feed fish, seabirds and whales.

nodes.name: Pacific herring
nodes.desc: Schooling fish that eats zooplankton and is prey for sea lions, whales and eagles.

nodes.name: Pacific salmon
nodes.desc: Spawn in the more than 100 salmon streams of Gwaii Haanas, carrying ocean nutrients into the forest.

nodes.name: Ancient murrelet
nodes.desc: A burrow-nesting seabird; about half the world population breeds on Haida Gwaii. Eats small fish and crustaceans.

nodes.name: Black rat
nodes.desc: Introduced by ships. Rats eat seabird eggs and chicks, and have devastated murrelet colonies. Eradication has been carried out on some Gwaii Haanas islands.

nodes.name: Common raven
nodes.desc: Clever scavenger that feeds on carcasses such as spawned-out salmon and deer.

nodes.name: Steller sea lion
nodes.desc: Large eared seal that eats fish such as herring and salmon, and is prey for orcas.

nodes.name: Humpback whale
nodes.desc: Feeds in the waters around Gwaii Haanas on krill and small schooling fish, which makes the area a key feeding habitat.

nodes.name: Haida Gwaii black bear
nodes.desc: Largest native land mammal of the archipelago. Eats salmon, shellfish and plants, and carries salmon remains into the forest.

nodes.name: Bald eagle
nodes.desc: Nests in coastal trees. Takes fish and seabirds, and scavenges.

nodes.name: Orca
nodes.desc: Top marine predator. Mammal-eating orcas hunt sea lions and whales; other orcas eat fish like salmon.
